about: THE NORWEGIAN KINGDOMS, 780-1070: from the sea-kings of the Karmsund and the kings of Vestfold to Harald Hardrada and his sons. Written 4 Oct 2026 for the dialogue and card writers; research, not a game table. rulers: one row per ruler and per 'part' (see parts), so the game can say who is king and who is the lord on the spot in any year; from/to are years. ports: who the two Norwegian port ids of ports_793.json (skiringssal, realm norse_vestfold; ogvaldsnes, realm norse_west) answer to, span by span. raids: 'where' is a port id from ports_793.json when the place is one, else a plain place name with 'near' (the nearest port id, where there is one). Raids by Northmen of Norway abroad and raids on Norway are both listed. certainty: sure / likely / uncertain, as in chronicle_793.json. There is no Norway and no king of it before about 900: the years given to the Vestfold kings of legend are modern guesses from counting generations, and Harald Fairhair's 872 is a 12th-century Icelandic reckoning. 'late' after a source means written in the 12th or 13th century about earlier days (the kings' sagas): good for colour, weak for fact. Chapter numbers of Heimskringla are given from memory and may be one or two out. (?) marks what could not be checked against the text itself on the night, or where the sources disagree. All dates Julian. Northmen is the sources' word; the word viking is not used.

abbreviations.ARF: Annales regni Francorum (ed. Kurze 1895), by year
abbreviations.ASC: Anglo-Saxon Chronicle, by manuscript and year; where quoted, J. Ingram's translation (1823) as printed by the Avalon Project (avalon.law.yale.edu/medieval/ang08.asp, ang11.asp; read 4 Oct 2026)
abbreviations.AU: Annals of Ulster, by year and entry
Annales Engolismenses, the Annals of Angouleme (MGH SS 16), by year
abbreviations.Adam: Adam of Bremen, Gesta Hammaburgensis ecclesiae pontificum (about 1075), by book and chapter
abbreviations.WJ: William of Jumieges, Gesta Normannorum ducum (about 1070), by book and chapter
abbreviations.JW: John of Worcester, Chronicle, by year
abbreviations.Ohthere: the account of Ohthere (Ottar) of Halogaland in the Old English Orosius, about 890
abbreviations.Ari: Ari Thorgilsson, Islendingabok (about 1125), by chapter: late, but careful, and the earliest Norse history
abbreviations.Hkv: Haraldskvaedi (Hrafnsmal), by Thorbjorn hornklofi, Harald Fairhair's own poet: about 900
abbreviations.Yt: Ynglingatal, by Thjodolf of Hvinir: a poem on the forefathers of a Vestfold king, about 900 (?); some put it in the 12th century
abbreviations.Vell: Vellekla, by Einar skalaglamm, on Jarl Hakon: about 986
abbreviations.Sigvat: Sigvat Thordarson, poet of Olaf Haraldsson and Magnus: Vikingarvisur, Nesjavisur, Austrfararvisur, Vestrfararvisur, the flokkr on Erling, Erfidrapa, Bersoglisvisur (about 1015-1040); an eyewitness
abbreviations.Agrip: Agrip af Noregskonungasogum (about 1190), by chapter: late
abbreviations.Hkr: Snorri Sturluson, Heimskringla (about 1230), by saga and chapter: late. Yng = Ynglinga saga, HSv = Halfdanar saga svarta, HHarf = Haralds saga harfagra, HGod = Hakonar saga goda, HGraf = Haralds saga grafeldar, OT = Olafs saga Tryggvasonar, OH = Olafs saga helga, MG = Magnuss saga goda, HS = Haralds saga Sigurdarsonar
abbreviations.Msk: Morkinskinna (about 1220), with the tale of Halldor Snorrason: late
abbreviations.Gragas: the Icelandic law book (13th-century manuscripts), which keeps the old agreement between King Olaf and the Icelanders
abbreviations.G: the older Gulathing law (written down in the late 11th or 12th century; whole only in a manuscript of about 1260), by chapter; read in L. M. Larson, The Earliest Norwegian Laws (1935): facts only, not quotable
abbreviations.DR 42: the great Jelling stone of Harald Bluetooth
abbreviations.Skre 2007: D. Skre (ed.), Kaupang in Skiringssal (Kaupang Excavation Project 1), Aarhus 2007
abbreviations.Skre 2008: D. Skre (ed.), Means of Exchange (Kaupang Excavation Project 2), Aarhus 2008: the coins, weights and hack-silver
abbreviations.Skre 2010: D. Skre, From Dorestad to Kaupang: Frankish traders and settlers in a 9th-century Scandinavian town (2010), as used in peoples/norse.md
abbreviations.Skre 2018: D. Skre (ed.), Avaldsnes: A Sea-Kings' Manor in First-Millennium Western Scandinavia, Berlin 2018 (?)
abbreviations.B&S 2009: N. Bonde and F.-A. Stylegar, Fra Avaldsnes til Oseberg, Viking 72 (2009): tree-ring dates of the ship graves (?)
abbreviations.Skaare: K. Skaare, Coins and Coinage in Viking-Age Norway (1976) and Norges mynthistorie (1995), as summarised on no.wikipedia.org/wiki/Penning and no.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harald_Hardråde (read 4 Oct 2026)
abbreviations.WP: en.wikipedia.org, the page named (read 4 Oct 2026): used for the conventional dates only

parts.danes: the king of the Danes as overlord of the Vik (the land round the Oslofjord, Vestfold in it): about 800-854, 970-986, 1000-1015, 1028-1035
parts.vestfold: the kings and under-kings in Vestfold and the Vik: the lord on the spot at skiringssal
parts.west: the sea-kings of Rogaland and Hordaland before there was one king: the lord on the spot at ogvaldsnes
parts.norway: the king of the Northmen, from Harald Fairhair on: at first a king of the west coast; a king of the whole land only from Olaf Haraldsson
parts.lade: the jarls of Hladir (Lade) by the Nid, lords of Trondelag and the north, who rule Norway in fact in 970-995 and 1000-1015

rulers.name: Sigfred
rulers.title: king of the Danes; overlord of Vestfold (?)
rulers.how_ended: last named in 798; Godfred is king by 804
rulers.source: ARF 777, 782, 798. That he held Vestfold is read back from ARF 813.

rulers.name: Godfred
rulers.title: king of the Danes; overlord of Vestfold. Skre holds that a Danish king, perhaps Godfred, laid out the market at Skíringssalr about 800
rulers.how_ended: murdered by one of his own men, 810

rulers.name: Hemming
rulers.title: king of the Danes; overlord of Vestfold
rulers.how_ended: died 812; a war for the kingship followed in which, the annals say, 10,940 men fell

rulers.name: Harald (Klak) and Reginfrid
rulers.title: kings of the Danes; overlords of Vestfold
rulers.how_ended: in 813 they took an army to Vestfold, the farthest part of their kingdom, lying north-west and looking to the north tip of Britain, whose chiefs and people would not obey them; that same year the sons of Godfred drove them out
rulers.source: ARF 813 (in our own words)

rulers.name: the sons of Godfred; Horik I alone from about 827
rulers.title: kings of the Danes; overlords of Vestfold (?)
rulers.how_ended: Horik was killed in a war with his nephew in 854 and the kingship fell apart. Nothing shows a Danish king holding the Vik again until Harald Bluetooth.

rulers.name: Halfdan the Mild (Halfdan hinn mildi ok hinn matarilli: open-handed with gold and stingy with food)
rulers.title: king in Vestfold, of the Yngling line (legend)
rulers.how_ended: died in his bed and was laid in a mound at Borre
rulers.source: Yt; Hkr Yng 47 (late). The years are a guess.

rulers.name: Gudrod the Hunter (Gudrodr veidikonungr)
rulers.title: king in Vestfold (legend)
rulers.how_ended: speared at night on the gangway of his ship by a servant of his wife Asa, whose father he had killed to get her
rulers.source: Yt; Hkr Yng 48 (late). The years are a guess. Not the Danish Godfred, though some have thought so.

rulers.name: Olaf Geirstad-Alf (Olafr Geirstadaalfr)
rulers.title: king in Vestfold (legend)
rulers.how_ended: died of a sickness in the leg and was laid in a mound at Geirstad. He is not the man in the Gokstad ship, who was buried about 901.
rulers.source: Yt; Hkr Yng 49 (late); for Gokstad, B&S 2009 (?). The years are a guess.

rulers.name: Halfdan the Black (Halfdan svarti)
rulers.title: king in Agder, the Uplands and half of Vestfold (saga); father of Harald Fairhair by the sagas
rulers.how_ended: drove home from a feast over the spring ice of the Randsfjord; the ice broke where cattle had been watered and he drowned with his men
rulers.source: Hkr HSv 9 (late); Agrip 1 (late). The years are a guess.

rulers.name: Ragnvald (Rognvaldr heidumhaeri)
rulers.title: king in Vestfold; the poem Ynglingatal was made for him
rulers.how_ended: not known; nothing is told of him but the poem's last verse
rulers.source: Yt; Hkr Yng 50 (late). The years are a guess.

rulers.name: Bjorn the Merchant (Bjorn farmadr, also called kaupmadr), a son of Harald Fairhair
rulers.title: under-king in Vestfold (saga)
rulers.how_ended: killed in his hall at Saeheim by his brother Eric Bloodaxe after refusing to hand over the king's dues. Snorri says he seldom went raiding, kept merchant ships and sent them to other lands for costly goods; his mound, the Farmannshaug, is shown at Sem.
rulers.source: Hkr HHarf 35 (late)

rulers.name: Gudrod Bjornsson in Vestfold; Tryggve Olafsson in the eastern Vik
rulers.title: under-kings of Hakon the Good (saga)
rulers.seat: Vestfold; the Vik east of the fjord
rulers.how_ended: both killed by the sons of Eric soon after Hakon's death: Tryggve lured to a meeting, Gudrod surprised at a feast
rulers.source: Hkr HGod 2, HGraf 9 (late)

rulers.name: Harald Grenske, son of Gudrod
rulers.title: under-king in Vestfold and Agder, holding them of Harald Bluetooth (saga); father of Olaf Haraldsson
rulers.how_ended: burned in a hall in Sweden, by the saga, when he came courting
rulers.source: Hkr OT 15, 43 (late)

rulers.name: the sea-kings at Ögvaldsnes; their names are lost
rulers.title: kings of the Rygir (?)
rulers.seat: Ögvaldsnes (Avaldsnes) on Karmoy, above the narrows of the Karmsund, where every ship on the coast road must pass
rulers.how_ended: the kings of the west were beaten by Harald at Hafrsfjord, and Ögvaldsnes became his farm
rulers.source: Two ship graves by the sound, dated by tree rings: Storhaug, buried 779, and Gronhaug, buried about 790-795 (B&S 2009); the manor dig (Skre 2018)

rulers.name: Kjotvi the Rich and Haklang; Eirik of Hordaland and Sulki of Rogaland
rulers.title: the kings who met Harald at Hafrsfjord
rulers.how_ended: beaten in the sea-fight in Hafrsfjord: Haklang fell, Kjotvi fled to an islet, and the wounded ran home over Jaeren with their minds on the mead-cup (the poem, in our words). Eirik and Sulki are named, and killed, only by Snorri.
rulers.source: Hkv 7-12; Hkr HHarf 18 (late)

rulers.name: Harald Fairhair (Haraldr harfagri; his own poet calls him Haraldr lufa, shock-head, and lord of the Northmen)
rulers.title: king of the west coast; by the sagas king of all Norway
rulers.seat: his farms on the west coast: Utstein (named by his poet), Ögvaldsnes, Fitjar, Alrekstad, Seim
rulers.how_ended: gave the high seat to his son Eric when he was old, died of sickness in Rogaland about three years later, and was laid in a mound at Haugar by the Karmsund
rulers.source: Hkv; Ohthere (the first written 'Nordweg', about 890; he names no king); Ari 1; Hkr HHarf 42-43 (late); WP List of Norwegian monarchs. Many now date Hafrsfjord to about 885-900 and doubt that he ever held the Vik.

rulers.name: Eric Bloodaxe (Eirikr blodox)
rulers.title: king
rulers.how_ended: driven out when his young brother Hakon came from England and the chiefs went over to him; sailed west. The sagas make him the Eric who was king at York and was killed on Stainmore in 954.
rulers.source: Agrip 5 (late); Hkr HGod 1-3 (late); ASC (D/E) 948, 954

rulers.name: Hakon the Good (Hakon Adalsteinsfostri, Athelstan's foster-son)
rulers.title: king
rulers.seat: the west-coast farms: Ögvaldsnes (953), Fitjar, Alrekstad, Seim
rulers.how_ended: hit in the arm by an arrow at Fitjar on Stord while beating the sons of Eric; died on the way north at the rock now called Hakonshella and was laid in a mound at Seim with his weapons, as a heathen
rulers.source: Eyvind skaldaspillir, Hakonarmal (about 961); Agrip 5-6 (late); Hkr HGod 28-32 (late); WP Haakon the Good

rulers.name: Sigurd Hakonarson
rulers.title: jarl of Hladir, lord of Trondelag under Hakon the Good
rulers.how_ended: burned in a hall at Aglo in Stjordal by the sons of Eric
rulers.source: Kormak, Sigurdardrapa (about 960); Hkr HGraf 5 (late)

rulers.name: Harald Greycloak (Haraldr grafeldr) with his brothers and their mother Gunnhild
rulers.title: king
rulers.how_ended: lured to Denmark and killed at Hals in the Limfjord by Gold-Harald, in a plot of Harald Bluetooth and Jarl Hakon
rulers.source: Glum Geirason, Grafeldardrapa (about 970); Hkr HGraf, OT 13-14 (late)

rulers.name: Harald Bluetooth
rulers.title: king of the Danes; overlord of Norway, holding the Vik himself
rulers.how_ended: Jarl Hakon stopped paying him after the German war of 974; Harald died of wounds about 986 after his son Sweyn rose against him
rulers.source: DR 42: the stone says he won for himself all Denmark and Norway and made the Danes Christian; Vell; Adam ii.25-28

rulers.name: Hakon Sigurdsson (Hakon jarl)
rulers.title: jarl of Hladir; ruler of western and northern Norway, at first under Harald Bluetooth, his own master from about 975
rulers.how_ended: the farmers of Trondelag rose against him as Olaf Tryggvason landed; he hid in a pit under a pigsty at Rimul in Gauldal, where his thrall Kark cut his throat
rulers.source: Vell (about 986); Agrip 12-13 (late); Hkr OT 48-49 (late); WP Haakon Sigurdsson

rulers.name: Olaf Tryggvason
rulers.title: king
rulers.seat: Nidaros, which he founded by the mouth of the Nid in 997 (Snorri)
rulers.how_ended: caught with few ships by Sweyn of Denmark, Olof of the Svear and Jarl Eirik at Svolder; leapt overboard from the Long Serpent. 9 September 1000 by Icelandic tradition; 999 by another reckoning.
rulers.source: Hallfred, Olafsdrapa and Erfidrapa (about 996-1001); Ari 7; Adam ii.40; Hkr OT (late)

rulers.name: Sweyn Forkbeard
rulers.title: king of the Danes; overlord of Norway, holding the Vik himself
rulers.how_ended: died at Gainsborough, 3 February 1014, weeks after winning England
rulers.source: Adam ii.41; ASC (C/D/E) 1014; Hkr OT 113 (late)

rulers.name: Eirik Hakonarson
rulers.title: jarl; ruler of the west coast and the north under Sweyn
rulers.how_ended: called to England by Cnut; left his young son Hakon in his place, whom Olaf Haraldsson caught in Saudungssund in 1015 and let go on his oath. Eirik was made earl of Northumbria in 1016 and died about 1023.
rulers.source: Thord Kolbeinsson, Eiriksdrapa (about 1016); ASC (C/D/E) 1016; Hkr OH 30 (late)

rulers.name: Svein Hakonarson
rulers.title: jarl; held his share of Norway of King Olof of the Svear
rulers.seat: Trondelag; Snorri says he set up a market at Steinker
rulers.how_ended: beaten by Olaf Haraldsson off Nesjar on Palm Sunday, 25 March 1016; fled east and died that autumn
rulers.source: Sigvat, Nesjavisur; Hkr OH 49-55 (late)

rulers.name: Olaf Haraldsson (Olaf the Stout; Saint Olaf after 1031)
rulers.title: king: the first to hold the whole land, coast and Uplands
rulers.seat: Nidaros; Borg by the Sarp falls, which he built in 1016
rulers.how_ended: the chiefs took Cnut's silver and Cnut came with a fleet in 1028; Olaf left his ships in a fjord, walked over the mountains and wintered with Yaroslav in Novgorod. He came back and was killed by the farmers' army at Stiklestad, 29 July 1030.
rulers.source: Sigvat; ASC (E) 1028, (C/D) 1030; Adam ii.57-61; Hkr OH (late); WP Olaf II of Norway

rulers.name: Cnut
rulers.title: king of England, Denmark and Norway
rulers.how_ended: died at Shaftesbury, 12 November 1035. His son Svein had already been driven from Norway.
rulers.source: ASC 1028: 'This year went King Knute from England to Norway with fifty ships manned with English thanes, and drove King Olave from the land, which he entirely secured to himself.' (Ingram 1823); ASC (C/D/E) 1035

rulers.name: Hakon Eiriksson
rulers.title: jarl; Cnut's regent in Norway
rulers.how_ended: drowned in the Pentland Firth coming home from England, late 1029 or 1030: the last jarl of Lade. Norway had no ruler on the spot until after Stiklestad.
rulers.source: ASC (C) 1030; Hkr OH 184 (late)

rulers.name: Svein Knutsson (Svein Alfifuson), a boy, with his mother Aelfgifu of Northampton (Alfiva)
rulers.title: king under his father Cnut
rulers.how_ended: the chiefs fetched Olaf's son Magnus from Russia; Svein and his mother fled to Denmark in 1034 or 1035, and he died there soon after. The years were remembered as Alfiva's time.
rulers.source: Agrip 28-32 (late); Hkr OH 239, MG 4 (late); WP Svein Knutsson

rulers.name: Magnus the Good (Magnus Olafsson)
rulers.title: king; also king of the Danes from 1042
rulers.how_ended: died in Denmark, 25 October 1047, aged about twenty-three, leaving Norway to his uncle Harald and Denmark to Sweyn Estridsen
rulers.source: Adam ii.77-79, iii.12; Sigvat, Bersoglisvisur; Hkr MG (late); WP List of Norwegian monarchs

rulers.name: Harald Sigurdsson (Hardrada, hard ruler: a name the sagas give him later)
rulers.title: king: with Magnus from 1046, alone from 1047
rulers.seat: Nidaros; Oslo, which the sagas say he founded about 1050 as a base against Denmark
rulers.how_ended: killed at Stamford Bridge near York, 25 September 1066
rulers.source: ASC (C/D/E) 1066; Adam iii.13, 17; Hkr HS (late); WP Harald Hardrada

rulers.name: Magnus Haraldsson
rulers.title: king: left to rule when his father sailed in 1066; from 1067 he holds the north and west, his brother Olaf the Vik
rulers.how_ended: died of sickness, 28 April 1069 (?)
rulers.source: Hkr HS 98-101 (late); WP List of Norwegian monarchs

rulers.name: Olaf Haraldsson the Quiet (Olaf kyrri)
rulers.title: king: with his brother from 1067, alone from 1069
rulers.seat: the Vik; later Bergen, which the sagas say he founded about 1070
rulers.how_ended: died of sickness, 22 September 1093, after twenty-six years without a war
rulers.source: ASC (D) 1066 (sent home from Stamford Bridge with 24 ships); Hkr, Olafs saga kyrra (late); WP List of Norwegian monarchs

spans.lord: a king of Vestfold with his hall at Huseby above the market; by legend Halfdan the Mild, then Gudrod the Hunter. The market's plots are laid out about 800; a jetty timber was felled in 803.

spans.king: danes: the army of 813 forces Vestfold to obey; how long it lasted is not known
spans.lord: the chiefs of Vestfold; by legend Olaf Geirstad-Alf. The Oseberg ship is buried a day's sail up the fjord in 834.
the kings of Vestfold (Ragnvald, by legend). A Frankish or Frisian trading household lives in the town until about the time Dorestad fails (Skre 2010). Ohthere puts in here about 890.

spans.king: norway, by the sagas (?): Harald Fairhair, then Hakon the Good
spans.lord: under-kings of the Vik: Bjorn the Merchant, then Gudrod Bjornsson (saga). The year-round town thins to a summer market about 930 and is gone by about 960, which is where ports_793.json ends it.
the sea-king at Ögvaldsnes, name lost: he watches the Karmsund and takes his due of what passes

spans.king: norway: Harald Fairhair, then Eric Bloodaxe
spans.lord: the king himself when he is at the farm; his steward (armadr) when he is not
the king or his steward. The sons of Eric are beaten here in 953.

spans.king: norway: Harald Greycloak and his brothers
lade: Jarl Hakon; over him Harald Bluetooth until about 975
norway: Olaf Tryggvason, who keeps Easter here in 998 (saga)
spans.lord: the king's steward; Erling Skjalgsson of Sola, the king's brother-in-law, holds the coast from the Sognefjord to Lindesnes

spans.king: lade: Jarl Eirik; over him Sweyn of Denmark
spans.lord: Erling Skjalgsson of Sola, in fact his own master
the king's steward Thorir Sel (killed here at Easter, about 1023); after him Asbjorn's kin and the king's men; Erling Skjalgsson close by at Sola until he is killed off Bokn, 21 December 1028

spans.king: danes: Cnut, through Jarl Hakon (to 1029), then Svein and Alfiva
spans.lord: the king's steward; the sons of Erling at Sola

spans.king: norway: Magnus Haraldsson (to 1069), then Olaf the Quiet

wars.who: Harald and Reginfrid, kings of the Danes, against the chiefs and people of Vestfold
wars.what: The two kings are away with their army in Vestfold, which will not obey them, when the emperor's envoys come to make peace. They force it to submit, and come home to find the sons of Godfred risen against them.
wars.what_it_did_to_trade: A Danish army sits on the Vik for a summer: stay away from Skíringssalr in 813. It also shows whose market it is: the dues there go, in the end, to the king of the Danes.

wars.who: Harald Fairhair against the kings of Hordaland, Rogaland and Agder
wars.what: Years of fighting along the coast (saga), ended by the sea-fight in Hafrsfjord. His poet saw the enemy come: ships from the east with gaping heads and carved prows, loaded with men and white shields, western spears and Frankish swords.
wars.what_it_did_to_trade: One king holds the Karmsund and the coast road north of it and takes what the small kings took. Chiefs who will not have him sell up and sail for Shetland, Orkney, the Hebrides and Iceland: for some years land and stock go cheap in the west, and a passage over sea is worth silver.
wars.source: Hkv 7-12; Ari 1-2; Hkr HHarf (late). 872 is the Icelandic reckoning; perhaps about 885-900.

wars.who: Eric Bloodaxe against his brothers, then Hakon against Eric
wars.what: Eric kills his brother Bjorn the Merchant in Vestfold and two more in Trondelag (saga). Hakon, fifteen and raised at King Athelstan's court, lands in Trondelag; Jarl Sigurd and the farmers take him as king, and Eric sails west without a fight.
wars.what_it_did_to_trade: The merchant-king of the Vik is dead and his ships scattered (saga). Hakon wins the farmers by giving back the land rights his father took (saga): lighter dues for a time, and a king who knows English ways.

wars.who: Hakon the Good against the sons of Eric, who have ships and men from Harald Bluetooth
wars.what: Three landings from Denmark, three battles: on Karmoy by Ögvaldsnes (953), at Rastarkalv on Frei (955), at Fitjar on Stord (961), where Hakon wins and dies of an arrow wound.
wars.what_it_did_to_trade: Fleets from Denmark raid the Vik and the west coast in summer. Hakon divides the coast into ship-districts and sets beacons on the heights (saga): when the fires are lit every harbour empties of men. In 953 the fight is at the king's farm at Ögvaldsnes itself.
wars.source: Guthorm sindri, Hakonardrapa (about 955); Eyvind, Hakonarmal (about 961); Hkr HGod 19-32 (late); WP Haakon the Good

wars.who: the sons of Eric against the jarl of Lade and the under-kings of the Vik
wars.what: Harald Greycloak and his brothers burn Jarl Sigurd in his hall (962), kill Tryggve and Gudrod in the Vik (963), and sail north round the cape to plunder Bjarmaland on the Dvina (about 965). Harald is killed in the Limfjord in 970.
wars.what_it_did_to_trade: Hungry years. The king's poet Eyvind says it snowed at midsummer and the goats were kept in like the Finns', and that he bought herring with his arrows and with the cloak-pin the Icelanders had sent him. Corn, malt and fish are worth more than silver; the kings are said to bury their gold rather than give it. Skíringssalr's last market falls in these years.
wars.source: Eyvind skaldaspillir's loose verses (about 965-970), kept in Hkr HGraf 16 (late); Glum Geirason, Grafeldardrapa; Skre 2007 for the end of the market

wars.who: Emperor Otto II against Harald Bluetooth, with Jarl Hakon's Norwegians on the Danish side
wars.what: Hakon brings a fleet south to hold the Danevirke; the emperor breaks through and sets a garrison in the march. Hakon is made to take baptism, puts the priests ashore on the way home, and pays Denmark nothing more. Danish ships then burn farms along the west coast (saga).
wars.what_it_did_to_trade: The crossing of Jutland at Sliesthorp is in German hands until 983. Norway pays no Danish tribute for twenty years. By his poet the earth grows again as it did before; Snorri adds that the herring came in along the whole coast.
wars.source: Vell; Thietmar of Merseburg iii.6; Hkr OT 16, 24-28 (late)

wars.who: a Danish fleet with the warriors of Jomsborg against Jarl Hakon and his son Eirik
wars.what: Beaten in Hjorungavag in Sunnmore, in a hailstorm the sagas made much of.
wars.what_it_did_to_trade: The Danish claim to the west coast is dead for a time. The Vik still looks to Denmark.
wars.source: Tind Hallkelsson, Hakonardrapa (about 987); Jomsvikinga saga (late). The year is a guess.

wars.who: Olaf Tryggvason and the farmers of Trondelag against Jarl Hakon
wars.what: Olaf comes from the west with English silver and a few ships as the farmers rise against the jarl for taking their wives and daughters (saga). Hakon dies in a pigsty; Olaf is made king at the thing.
wars.what_it_did_to_trade: A Christian king who has seen London: he lays out Nidaros as a market in 997 (Snorri) and strikes the first Norwegian pennies. Heathen crews are held in harbour until they are baptised.

wars.who: Sweyn of Denmark, Olof of the Svear and Jarl Eirik against Olaf Tryggvason
wars.what: The sea-fight at Svolder: Olaf, sailing home from Wendland with eleven ships (?), is cut off and leaps from the Long Serpent.
wars.what_it_did_to_trade: Norway is shared three ways: the Vik to the Danish king, a share to the king of the Svear through Jarl Svein, the west and north to Jarl Eirik. Nobody presses the faith. Fifteen quiet years, in which Northmen go to England with Sweyn and Cnut and come home with English pennies.
wars.source: Hallfred, Erfidrapa (about 1001); Ari 7; Adam ii.40; Hkr OT 97-113 (late)

wars.who: Olaf Haraldsson against the jarls of Lade
wars.what: Olaf comes from England with two merchant ships and a little over two hundred men (saga) (?), catches young Jarl Hakon in Saudungssund, and beats Jarl Svein off Nesjar on Palm Sunday, 25 March 1016. His poet Sigvat was aboard.
wars.what_it_did_to_trade: The battle is fought off the Vestfold shore, near where Skíringssalr's market had been. After it there is one king over coast and Uplands for the first time. He builds Borg at the Sarp falls (1016) to hold the Vik against Svear and Danes, and takes the dues there himself.
wars.source: Sigvat, Nesjavisur; Hkr OH 29-30, 49-61 (late); WP Olaf II of Norway

wars.who: Olaf Haraldsson against Olof, king of the Svear
wars.what: Killings of tax-gatherers on the border and a closed frontier, ended when Sigvat rides east through the forest to Jarl Ragnvald in Gautland; Olaf marries King Olof's daughter Astrid in 1019.
wars.what_it_did_to_trade: The trade between the Vik and Gautland is shut for three years. By Snorri both sides begged for peace because of it: the Gauts could get no herring or salt (?). Sigvat found the forest farms shut too: at one after another the people were holding a sacrifice to the elves and turned the Christians away.

wars.who: Cnut against Olaf Haraldsson and Anund of the Svear
wars.what: Olaf and Anund raid Denmark while Cnut is in England and meet him at the Holy River in Skane (1026). Cnut then sends silver to the Norwegian chiefs, comes with a fleet in 1028 and is taken as king at the thing in Trondelag without a blow. Erling Skjalgsson of Sola, the great man of the west coast, is cut down off Bokn on 21 December 1028, in the one fight of the war.
wars.what_it_did_to_trade: English pennies in every chief's chest: Sigvat says Cnut's envoys went about with open purses. From 1028 to 1035 one king holds London, Ribe and Nidaros, and the North Sea is as safe as it ever gets. The fight off Bokn is a morning's sail south of Ögvaldsnes.
wars.source: ASC (E) 1025 (=1026), 1028; JW 1027; Sigvat, Vestrfararvisur and the flokkr on Erling; Hkr OH 145-176 (late)

wars.who: Olaf Haraldsson, back from Russia, against the farmers and chiefs of Trondelag and the north
wars.what: Stiklestad in Verdal, 29 July 1030. 'This year returned King Olave into Norway; but the people gathered together against him, and fought against him; and he was there slain, in Norway, by his own people, and was afterwards canonised.' (ASC, Ingram 1823)
wars.what_it_did_to_trade: Nothing at sea. But from 1031 Nidaros has a saint's shrine, and pilgrims are a trade: wax, wine for the Mass, lodging, and passages north.

wars.who: Svein Knutsson against a man calling himself Tryggve, son of Olaf Tryggvason
wars.what: Tryggve comes from the west over sea with ships; Svein meets him in Soknasund in Rogaland and kills him.
wars.what_it_did_to_trade: A sea-fight in the sounds south of Ögvaldsnes, and a sign of how thin Svein's hold is: two years later he is gone.

wars.who: Magnus, king of Norway and Denmark, against the Wends and against Sweyn Estridsen
wars.what: By a treaty with Harthacnut the longer-lived of the two was to have both kingdoms. Magnus takes Denmark in 1042, burns Jomsborg at the Oder mouth (1043), breaks a great Wendish army on Lyrskov Heath by Sliesthorp (28 September 1043), and fights Sweyn at sea summer after summer.
wars.what_it_did_to_trade: One king over Nidaros, Ribe and Sliesthorp; the Danish mints strike in his name. The Wendish raids on Jutland stop. But the Danish waters are a war zone each summer from 1043.
wars.source: Adam ii.77-79; Arnor jarlaskald, Magnusdrapa and Hrynhenda (about 1046); Hkr MG (late)

wars.who: Harald Sigurdsson against Sweyn Estridsen, king of the Danes
wars.what: Seventeen summers of raids on Jutland and the Danish isles. Hedeby is burned from end to end (1049 or 1050). The Danish fleet is beaten at the mouth of the Nisa in Halland on 9 August 1062 and Sweyn gets ashore alive. In 1064 the two kings meet on the Gota river and each keeps what he has.
wars.what_it_did_to_trade: Sliesthorp never recovers: its trade moves over the Schlei to Schleswig. A Norwegian ship in Danish water, or a Danish one in the Vik, is a prize. Harald pays his men in thin pennies (see coins). Oslo grows as his base at the head of the fjord.
wars.source: Thorleik fagri and Stein Herdisarson (verses, about 1050-1062); Adam iii.13 (?); Hkr HS 34, 58, 61-71 (late); WP Harald Hardrada

wars.who: Harald Sigurdsson against Jarl Hakon Ivarsson and the farmers of the Uplands
wars.what: The Upland farmers hold back the king's dues; he burns their farms in Romerike, Hedmark and Ringerike.
wars.what_it_did_to_trade: Inland only. Iron, whetstones and furs from the Uplands come down to the Vik late or not at all for two years (our inference).

wars.who: Harald Sigurdsson and Earl Tostig against England
wars.what: Harald sails with about 300 ships by Shetland and Orkney, joins Tostig, burns Scarborough (saga), beats the earls at Fulford by York on 20 September and takes hostages from the city. Five days later King Harold surprises him at Stamford Bridge. Twenty-four ships carry the living home.
wars.what_it_did_to_trade: The levy strips the coast of ships and men for a summer, and most do not come back. After it comes Olaf the Quiet's long peace: the best years for a merchant in the whole span.

raids.who: three ships of Northmen from Hordaland
raids.what: The king's reeve Beaduheard rides down from Dorchester, takes them for traders and orders them to the king's town; they kill him. 'And in his days came first three ships of the Northmen from the land of robbers.' (ASC, Ingram 1823; 'the land of robbers' is his reading of Haeretha land, Hordaland.)
raids.source: ASC (D/E/F) 787 (=789); Aethelweard iii.1 for the reeve's name and Dorchester

raids.who: heathen men; their home is not named. The Hordaland ships of 789 and the Irish and English church metalwork in west Norwegian graves make the west coast the usual guess (?)
raids.what: 8 June: Saint Cuthbert's church plundered, monks killed, drowned or carried off.

raids.who: the same heathen men
raids.what: The monastery at the mouth of the Don is plundered. One of their chiefs is killed, a storm breaks up some of the ships, and the crews are killed as they come ashore.

raids.who: heathens, by the Irish annals: ships come round the north of Scotland by Shetland and Orkney
raids.what: Iona plundered, and Rechru burned and its shrines broken, in one year.

raids.where: Inis Patraic, an island church north of the Liffey
raids.who: heathens
raids.what: They burn the church, break the shrine of Do Chonna and take a cattle-tribute from the mainland: the first tribute, not only plunder.

raids.who: heathens
raids.what: Iona was burned in 802; in 806 sixty-eight of the community are killed. The abbot moves the house to Kells (807-814).

raids.who: Harald and Reginfrid, kings of the Danes
raids.what: An army in Vestfold to make its chiefs obey (see wars).

raids.who: heathens
raids.what: The monk Blathmac is killed for refusing to say where Columba's shrine is buried.
raids.source: AU 825.17; Walafrid Strabo's poem on Blathmac

raids.who: a fleet of Northmen
raids.what: A ship-fort is built at Duiblinn and held through the winter: the start of the town, and from now on the market where the west-coast Northmen sell captives.

raids.who: 'Westfaldingi', men of Vestfold: the one fleet in the Frankish annals called by the name of a Norwegian land
raids.what: They storm Nantes on Saint John's day, 24 June, kill Bishop Gunhard in his church, and winter on Noirmoutier.
raids.source: Ann. Engol. 843 (the name); Chronicle of Nantes; Annales Bertiniani 843 (which says only Northmen)

raids.who: Amlaib (Olaf), son of the king of Laithlind
raids.what: He comes to Ireland; the foreigners there submit to him and the Irish pay him tribute. Laithlind is Norway, or the Norse lands in the Scottish isles (?).

raids.who: Ingimund's Northmen, driven out of Dublin in 902
raids.what: Given land by Chester by the lady Aethelflaed, they try to take the city; the story has the townsmen pour hot ale and throw beehives on them. Aethelflaed restores the walls in 907.
raids.source: Fragmentary Annals of Ireland (11th century; legend in the detail) (?); ASC (C) 907

raids.who: the sons of Eric Bloodaxe, with ships from Denmark
raids.what: They land on Karmoy while King Hakon is at his farm at Ögvaldsnes. He beats them on the ridge above the sound; Guthorm Eiriksson is killed and the rest flee to their ships.
raids.source: Hkr HGod 19-20 (late); WP Avaldsnes; WP Haakon the Good

raids.where: Bjarmaland: the mouth of the Dvina, off the chart
raids.who: Harald Greycloak
raids.what: He sails north round the cape and fights on the bank of the Vina. The furs come home as plunder, not as trade.
raids.source: Glum Geirason, Grafeldardrapa (about 970); Hkr HGraf 14 (late). The year is a guess.

raids.who: a northern ship-army: from the Irish Sea or the isles; the Chronicle says only northern
raids.what: Cheshire is ravaged.

raids.where: the coasts of Saxony, Frisia, Walcheren and Flanders
raids.who: Olaf Tryggvason, before he was king
raids.what: His poet counts the peoples he fought on his way west: Saxons, Frisians, the men of Walcheren (?), Flemings; then the English, Scots, Manx and Irish. For a Frisian house this is the Norwegian king who fed the wolves on Frisians.
raids.source: Hallfred, Olafsdrapa (about 996), as used in peoples/norse.md. The years are a guess: some time in 985-991.

raids.who: Olaf with 93 ships (one text of the Chronicle names him)
raids.what: Folkestone, Sandwich and Ipswich are ravaged; Ealdorman Byrhtnoth is killed at Maldon; 10,000 pounds are paid.

raids.who: Olaf Tryggvason and Sweyn of Denmark, with 94 ships
raids.what: They try to burn London on 8 September and are driven off, then winter at Southampton on 16,000 pounds. Olaf is confirmed at Andover with King Aethelred as sponsor, promises never to come back in war, and keeps his word: the silver pays for his kingdom.

raids.where: Kinnlimasida: the Kennemer coast of Frisia (?)
raids.who: Olaf Haraldsson, a boy of about fourteen, with his foster-father Hrani steering for him (saga)
raids.what: His fifth fight, by his poet's count: riders come down to the shore against the ships and are driven off.
raids.source: Sigvat, Vikingarvisur 5. The year is a guess (1008 or 1009).

raids.who: Olaf Haraldsson, with Thorkell's army
raids.what: His sixth fight is at London's bridge. Snorri's tale that he roofed his ships with wicker and pulled the bridge down with cables is told of 1014 and of the English side (late).
raids.source: Sigvat, Vikingarvisur 6; Ottar the Black, Hofudlausn (about 1023); ASC (C/D/E) 1009-1010; Hkr OH 12-13 (late); WP Olaf II of Norway

raids.who: Thorkell's army, Olaf Haraldsson in it
raids.what: Canterbury, whose port Fordwic is, is taken in September after a siege and Archbishop Aelfheah carried off. Sigvat counts it Olaf's eighth fight.

raids.who: Harald Sigurdsson
raids.what: Hedeby is burned from end to end. One of his men made a verse of standing on the town wall before dawn, watching the flames rise from the houses.
raids.source: an unnamed poet's verse and Thorleik fagri's, kept in Hkr HS 34 (late); chronicle_793.json puts it in 1050

raids.where: the Irish Sea and the Welsh march
raids.who: a fleet from Norway under Magnus, King Harald's young son, with ships from Orkney, the Isles and Dublin
raids.what: It helps the outlawed Earl Aelfgar and Gruffydd of Wales force Aelfgar's return. The English chronicler says only that a ship-army came from Norway and that it would be tedious to tell how it all went.
raids.source: ASC (D) 1058 (in our words); Annals of Tigernach 1058; Annales Cambriae 1058

raids.who: Harald Sigurdsson with about 300 ships, and Earl Tostig
raids.what: Cleveland is harried and Scarborough burned (saga); the earls are beaten at Fulford on 20 September and York gives hostages and food. On the 25th the Norwegians, without their mail, are caught at Stamford Bridge.

laws.what: No king's law reaches a stranger. Each land has its thing of free men. Vestfold's meets at Thjodalyng (Tjolling), a short walk from the market at Skíringssalr, below the king's hall at Huseby.
laws.what_it_means_for_a_merchant: Your safety is your host: a man of the place who answers for you. Find him before you unload, and give him a gift worth his trouble. Inside the market the peace is the king's, kept by his steward.
laws.source: Skre 2007 (the hall, the thing site, the market) (?)

laws.what: Frankish law, not Norse, but it binds a Frisian: no swords or mail to be sold beyond the border posts (805); on pain of death from 864.
laws.what_it_means_for_a_merchant: The thing a Northman most wants from your hold is the thing you may not sell him. Frankish swords are in Harald Fairhair's enemies' ships all the same.
laws.source: MGH Capit. I no. 44 c. 7; Edict of Pitres (864) c. 25; Hkv 8; realms/francia.json

laws.what: The tribute of the Finnas (the Sami) belongs to the great men of the north. Each Finn pays by his rank: the highest fifteen marten skins, five reindeer skins, one bear skin, ten measures of feathers, a coat of bear or otter skin and two ship's ropes sixty ells long, one of walrus hide and one of seal.
laws.what_it_means_for_a_merchant: Walrus tooth, hide rope, furs and down reach the southern markets only through such men. You cannot go and buy from the Finnas yourself. By the 1020s this trade is the king's (see 1026).

laws.what: King Harald, to stop the land emptying, sets a due on every man who sails from Norway to Iceland: five ounces of silver. It is the start of the toll called landaurar. Sometimes more was paid and sometimes less, until Olaf Haraldsson fixed it at half a mark for every man but women and those the king let off.
laws.what_it_means_for_a_merchant: Carrying settlers and their stock west is good freight, but the king's man counts heads at the harbour: five ounces a man, about 135 g of silver.
laws.source: Ari 1 (in our words). The year stands for about 880-930.

laws.what: By the sagas Harald took all inherited land for his own, made every farmer pay him land-dues, and set a jarl over each district to gather them and keep a third. Historians doubt the first part.
laws.what_it_means_for_a_merchant: On the west coast the man to pay is the king's steward at the king's farm, or the jarl: not a toll by tariff but a gift fitted to the cargo. In return the harbour below a king's farm is under his peace.

laws.what: The men of Hordaland, Sogn and the Fjords have one law, said at the Gulathing: when Iceland wanted a law, Ulfljot went to Norway and brought one home made mostly after the Gulathing law as it then was.
laws.what_it_means_for_a_merchant: On the west coast a quarrel goes to a thing with a known law. A stranger needs oath-helpers: three, six or twelve men who will swear beside him. The written law later gives a foreign trader a farmer's right (?).

laws.what: King Hakon sets the Gulathing law with Thorleif the Wise and the Frostathing law with Jarl Sigurd. He divides the whole coast into ship-districts, each to build, man and feed a warship for the levy, and has beacons built on the heights, so that word of a fleet runs from the south end of the land to the north in seven nights (saga). He also moves Yule to the days of Christmas and orders every man to brew a measure of malt for it.
laws.what_it_means_for_a_merchant: In a levy summer ships, sails and men are called out and no one loads cargo. Lit beacons mean an enemy fleet on the coast: stay in harbour. Malt sells well before Yule.
laws.source: Hkr HGod 11, 13, 20 (late); WP Haakon the Good (the levy linked to him in verse and saga)

laws.what: Olaf Tryggvason lays out a market town on the flat by the mouth of the Nid, gives men plots to build on, and builds a king's hall and a church there (Snorri).
laws.what_it_means_for_a_merchant: The first place north of the Danes where a ship can lie the winter under a king's peace, with a church. Dried fish, furs and walrus tooth from the north come here instead of being fetched farm by farm. It is north of the chart's two Norwegian ports: news of it, and its goods, reach Ögvaldsnes.

laws.what: Olaf Tryggvason has each thing choose between baptism and battle; those who refuse are driven out, maimed or killed (saga). Icelanders lying in Nidaros are held and threatened until Iceland takes the faith (999-1000).
laws.what_it_means_for_a_merchant: A heathen shipmaster in a Norwegian harbour takes baptism, or at least the first signing, or does not sail. A Christian Frisian is suddenly a welcome man.
laws.source: Ari 7; Oddr Snorrason, Olafs saga (late); Hkr OT 53-84 (late); Laxdaela saga 40-41 (late)

laws.what: The jarls Eirik and Svein are baptised men but let each man do as he will about the faith, and keep the old laws well (Snorri).
laws.what_it_means_for_a_merchant: Fifteen easy years: heathen and Christian crews trade side by side and nobody asks.

laws.what: In years of bad harvest in the north, King Olaf forbids corn, malt and meal to be carried out of Agder, Rogaland and Hordaland.
laws.what_it_means_for_a_merchant: The king's steward may seize a grain cargo going north past Ögvaldsnes, and the sail with it. Asbjorn of Halogaland got round the ban by buying from the thralls of Erling Skjalgsson, who were outside the law; the steward Thorir Sel took the corn anyway.
laws.source: Hkr OH 117-120 (late). The year is Snorri's reckoning.

laws.what: King Olaf's agreement with the Icelanders, the oldest treaty of the north that survives: an Icelander in Norway has the rights of a hauld (a freeholder of old family); he pays landaurar on landing, six cloaks and six ells of homespun or half a mark of silver, and no other toll; he may take wood and water in the king's forest; if the land is attacked while he is there he must help defend it; his goods wait in Norway for his heir.
laws.what_it_means_for_a_merchant: The model of a merchant's charter in the north: one named payment, then free of toll. A Frisian has no such treaty and stands on his host and the king's goodwill.
laws.source: Gragas, Konungsbok (?); Ari 1. The year is a guess: Olaf's reign, sworn to again by Icelanders later in the century.

laws.what: At a thing on the island of Moster, King Olaf and his English bishop Grimkel set the Christian law: children to be baptised and none exposed; no sacrifice to the old gods; no horse-meat; Sunday and the feast days kept free of work; Friday a fast; ale to be brewed and blessed at Christmas for a good year and peace; a thrall to be freed each year by the thing. The Gulathing law still cites it as what Saint Olaf and Bishop Grimkel laid down at the Moster thing. 1024 by tradition; 1022 if the Kuli stone counts from it.
laws.what_it_means_for_a_merchant: No loading, selling or sailing out on a Sunday or a feast day, on pain of a fine in silver to the bishop. No meat on a Friday in a Norwegian harbour. A crew that sacrifices for wind risks outlawry. Churches now stand at the things: places of sworn peace.
laws.source: G 10-29 (?); Hkr OH 58 (late); N 449; WP Kuli stone

laws.what: King Olaf sends Karli of Halogaland north to Bjarmaland with the king's goods, the two to share the gain half and half; Thorir Hund joins with his own ship. They buy grey fur, beaver and sable at the market on the Dvina, then, the truce over, rob the grave-field and the idol of the god Jomali.
laws.what_it_means_for_a_merchant: The far-north trade is the king's: a man sails in it as his partner or not at all. And a market truce there lasts only as long as the market.

laws.what: Alfiva's laws, after the Danish pattern but harsher: no man may leave the land without the king's leave, or his goods are forfeit; a killer loses land and goods; at Christmas each hearth gives the king a measure of malt, the thigh of a three-year ox and a pail of butter, and each housewife as much unspun flax as thumb and long finger can span; farmers build the king's houses; of every seven males over five one fits out a man for the levy; each man who rows out to fish pays the king five fish; every ship that leaves the land keeps a space across the hold for the king; every man who sails to Iceland pays landaurar, native or foreign; and the oath of one Dane outweighs ten Norwegians.
laws.what_it_means_for_a_merchant: The worst years. A room across your ship is the king's on every voyage out; your Norwegian partner cannot sail without leave; and in a suit against a Dane you have lost before you speak.
laws.source: Agrip 28-29 (late) (?); Hkr OH 239 (late), from memory of the text; WP Svein Knutsson

laws.what: Magnus begins by taking the farms of the men who fought his father. The farmers mutter of rising; the poet Sigvat, chosen by lot to tell him, makes the Plain-speaking Verses. The king gives way, and has a law written for Trondelag that was later called Grey Goose (Snorri).
laws.what_it_means_for_a_merchant: The takings stop and the feuds of 1030 are closed: safe to deal again with the great houses of Trondelag and the west.

laws.what: Harald makes the king's own penny the money of the land and thins its silver from about nine parts in ten to under three; foreign coin goes out of use (see coins).
laws.what_it_means_for_a_merchant: Sell for the king's pennies and a good part of your price is copper: hold out for weighed silver or for goods. His own man Halldor Snorrason threw his pay on the floor.

laws.what: In a famine year in Iceland, King Harald lets four ships sail there with meal and sets the price: a ship-pound for no more than a hundred of homespun. He lets poor men who can find their own food for the crossing leave Iceland for Norway.
laws.what_it_means_for_a_merchant: A king can set the price of your cargo before you sail. Grain to Iceland goes by the king's leave.
laws.source: Hkr HS 36 (late). The year is from the Icelandic annals' famine (?).

coins.what: No coin of their own. Silver goes by weight: rings, bars and cut pieces, weighed on folding scales against lead and bronze weights and nicked to test it. The mark is about 214 g, of 8 ounces. At Skíringssalr goods were at first paid for mostly in kind; cut silver and weights are common there from the middle of the 800s (?).

Arab dirhams, whole and cut, come west from the Baltic and are found at Skíringssalr; a few Frankish and English pennies come too, and a gold coin of Dorestad. Foreign coins are silver, not money: many are fitted with a loop and worn. The Hon hoard in Buskerud (buried after about 860 (?)) is 2.5 kg of gold, with Frankish, Arab, Byzantine and English coins all made into pendants.
coins.mints: none: Islamic mints far to the east; Dorestad
coins.source: Skre 2008; WP Kaupang (Arab silver coins, a gold coin from Dorestad); the Hon hoard from memory (?)

coins.what: English pennies of Aethelred II and Cnut, from the tributes and from pay, and German pennies fill the hoards; pennies of the Frisian counts are among the German coin (?). They are still weighed and nicked.
coins.mints: none in Norway: London, Winchester, York and the rest of the English mints; Cologne, Goslar and the German mints

coins.what: Olaf Tryggvason's penny, the first Norwegian coin: a copy of Aethelred's Crux type, reading ONLAF REX NOR, with the English moneyer's name GODWINE on the other side. Four are known, in Stockholm, Lund, Copenhagen and Berlin: none was found in Norway.
Olaf Haraldsson's pennies, again on English models and by English moneyers, naming him king of the Northmen. Few survive.
coins.source: Skaare (only from about 1025 can he be called the lord of the coin with any certainty); WP Olaf II of Norway (a coin dated 1023-1028)

coins.what: Magnus the Good strikes pennies as king of the Danes at the Danish mints. Whether any were struck in Norway is not settled.
coins.mints: Lund, Hedeby and other Danish mints (?)

coins.what: Harald Sigurdsson's penny: the first lasting coinage of Norway, about 0.9 g, 240 to the mark. At first about nine-tenths silver; after about 1055 under a third, the rest copper: 'Harald's striking' (Haraldsslatta). Foreign coin goes out of the hoards: the king's penny is the only money, and it passes by count, not weight.

Harald's sons go on striking the thin penny. A later reform (under Olaf the Quiet by one account, about 1095 by another (?)) brings the silver back to about nine-tenths and halves the weight to 0.44 g.

church.what: Hakon, baptised and raised at King Athelstan's court, comes home a Christian: the first Norwegian king who is. He keeps Sundays and the Friday fast in private (saga).

Hakon sends to England for a bishop and priests and asks the Trondelag farmers to take the faith. They refuse, burn three churches in More and kill the priests, and make him eat horse-liver at the Yule sacrifice at Maere (saga). HN calls him an apostate who served both God and the gods.
church.source: Hkr HGod 13-18 (late); HN (late); WP Haakon the Good

church.what: Hakon is laid in a mound at Seim with his weapons. His poet has the heathen gods welcome him to their hall because he spared the holy places.
The sons of Eric, baptised in England, pull down heathen shrines where they can but build nothing in their place; the bad seasons are blamed on it (saga).

Jarl Hakon, made to take baptism in Denmark after the German war, puts the priests ashore and sacrifices as soon as he lands. His poet praises him for giving the shrines back to the gods, so that the earth grows as before.
church.source: Vell (about 986); Hkr OT 27 (late); WP Haakon Sigurdsson

church.what: Olaf Tryggvason is confirmed at Andover by Bishop Aelfheah, with King Aethelred as his sponsor.
Olaf lands on the island of Moster in Sunnhordland and has Mass sung there in a tent; a church is built on the spot afterwards (saga).
church.source: Oddr Snorrason, Olafs saga (late); Hkr OT 47 (late)

church.what: Bones found in a cave on the island of Selja are taken for those of Sunniva, an Irish king's daughter, and her companions; a church is built there (saga).

The coast is baptised thing by thing, from the Vik round to Halogaland, by promise and by force. At Ögvaldsnes, by the saga, the king keeps Easter, has a band of sorcerers bound on a skerry that the tide covers, and is kept up late by an old one-eyed guest who knows too much about the dead king Ogvald.
Iceland takes the faith by law at the Althing, under the king's pressure, the summer he falls.
Olaf Haraldsson, raiding for Duke Richard II, is baptised at Rouen by the duke's brother, Archbishop Robert. (Snorri has him baptised as a child with Olaf Tryggvason for godfather.)
church.source: WJ v.11-12; WP Olaf II of Norway. The year is 1013 or 1014.

church.what: Olaf brings bishops and priests from England: Sigfrid, Grimkel, Rudolf and Bernhard. Grimkel is his court bishop.
The Christian law is set at the Moster thing (see laws).

3 August: a year and five days after Stiklestad, Bishop Grimkel has Olaf's body taken up at Nidaros, finds it whole with hair and nails grown, and declares him a saint with the leave of the king and the people. His feast is 29 July. Within a year a poet tells Svein that bells ring of themselves over the shrine and the blind and the lame go home healed.
church.source: Thorarin loftunga, Glaelognskvida (about 1032); Sigvat, Erfidrapa; Hkr OH 244 (late); WP Olaf II of Norway

church.what: Two men raise a stone on Kuli in Nordmore: 'twelve winters had Christendom been in Norway'. A plank road beside it was built of timber felled in 1034.
church.source: N 449; WP Kuli stone (the dating assumes stone and road are of one time)

church.what: 15 May (?): Hallvard, a merchant-farmer's son of Lier, is shot on the Drammen fjord defending a woman accused of theft, and sunk with a millstone that floats: Oslo's saint.
church.source: the legend of Saint Hallvard (late); peoples/norse.md

church.what: Harald has his bishops consecrated in England and France, not at Bremen, and takes the offerings at Saint Olaf's shrine for his own men. When Archbishop Adalbert's envoys protest, he answers that he knows of no archbishop or lord in Norway but Harald himself. The pope writes to him to obey.
church.source: Adam iii.17 (in our words); WP Harald Hardrada. The year stands for about 1053-1061.

church.what: Under Olaf the Quiet the bishops settle at fixed seats: Nidaros, Selja (soon Bergen) and Oslo. Adam, writing about 1075, still says the Norwegian bishops have no fixed bounds.
